Do you know what he meant? Do you know what happened in local communes that was supposed to be placed under control?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the ground in town itself there were several units -- well, groups. They weren't really units, that took part in this fighting. I already said that he tried, I think, to co-ordinate their activities, the activities over those few days. And there were some individuals or groups who were armed within JNA units, whereas others, individually or as groups, took part in these activities in town. Part of these units were in the settlements around town. Chaos prevailed during those days. Adventurers, criminals, all sorts of people showed up. And it was only later through the decisions of the president of the Assembly we tried to bring some order into all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By now Mauzer is deceased. Was he ever criminally charged with anything? Was an indictment ever issued against him?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that period I think. I don't know. His activities later in the MUP or something -- I mean ten years afterwards so I wouldn't go into that now. I think at that time there wasn't anything like that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mauzer, did he hold an official position after Dayton; and if so, what was that?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Dayton he was director of the police of Republika Srpska or some assistant minister of police of Republika Srpska, whatever the actual title may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could he have been that without certification from the international forces, the international police?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he couldn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested today to you on the basis of the "Los Angeles Times" and other newspapers that the Serb press adored Arkan. Did you ever read any text in which adoration for Arkan was expressed?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I mean, adoration, that's a bit over the top. There were -- there was criticism, there was praise. I read different things especially not then by April 1992, perhaps I followed these writings more afterwards, after April, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know and did Croatia take Arkan prisoner during their war?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, Arkan was well-known as the leader of the football fans of Crvena Zvezda and I think it was on that basis that he was arrested when the conflicts broke out in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many people did Arkan bring to Bijeljina, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during these four or five days I saw them twice, once when Fikret and Biljana came, and before that I saw them when I tried to calm things down when there was this conflict between these paramilitaries, or whatever you call them, on the one hand and the JNA on the other in town. It was on the 2nd, I think, and Biljana and Fikret were on the 3rd or 4th. So it was twice that we saw each other. And as for Biljana and Fikret's visit, they presented it in the media in their own way. I was searched when entering the Assembly. I think that "Vreme" or some Belgrade paper carried that at the time. They were saying that they were worried about security in front of the municipality building. There were 16 or 17 of them when Fikret and Biljana came. And on the 1st perhaps there was even less of them. They came to Bijeljina on the 1st, in my view probably at the invitation of members of Arkan's unit who were from the area around Bijeljina and joined in the fighting; I mean, probably that is my conclusion, that it was on that basis that they arrived in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it established whether there had been any fatalities before Arkan showed up in Bijeljina and what do you know? Were there any fatalities before Arkan entered Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to confirm that now, but during the evening, or rather, during the night in the centre of town about two persons lost their life. I know that for sure and Zeljko was not in Bijeljina at the time. Now, what happened during the following two days, although I think that most of the fatalities were people who lost their lives in the area around the city hospital. And it's only there that concrete fighting took place between these Serb and Muslim formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that point in time, who controlled the hospital?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four days or for three days these Muslim paramilitary formations held the hospital under their control in that part of town in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now take a look at P2919. I would like to ask you to take a look at those photographs about which you said that you were not sure as to whether it was Bijeljina at all. I would like to ask you to take a look at something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move away from this topic, as regards the video-clip which we admitted as Exhibit P6211, the transcript I saw while it was played was of five pages and I checked with it and now it's of ten pages without any redactions. Is it due to upgrade as well? So I would like the parties to check whether they are happy with it. I see -- myself see no difficulty with it, but I'll leave it to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And numerically that conforms to our understanding of what it should be, but we're happy to check the exact document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2919, please. It's a Prosecution exhibit, 02119.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Simic, is there a difference in terms of the way in which Muslim and Christian women dress in our part of the world? Can you tell anything on the basis of clothing?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is this traditional difference, but in Bijeljina, I mean, this classical Muslim attire of women is different but it doesn't mean that a large portion of the Muslim population dressed the same way. I mean, on that basis one cannot conclude what it may be. I don't know anyone in this photograph. So now on the basis of what can I claim anything? I'm not claiming that it's not in Bijeljina, but I cannot claim that it is in Bijeljina either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which ethnic community primarily wears black, especially women?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, black clothing is characteristic of Serbs, I think, older women. Muslim women wear a different kind of pants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember what the weather was like in early April and is this woman sufficiently dressed for weather like that?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was rather chilly. I wore an overcoat. Perhaps this woman just went out for a bit. I don't think she spent much time outdoors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page. 156 are the last digits of the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we know whether those who are lying on the ground are dead or alive?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't even who they were. How can I know whether they're alive or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of the clothing, can you infer anything?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that video footage Mauzer is speaking and he mentions the Crisis Staff of the SAO Semberija and Majevica. Semberija and Majevica, can one say that that is the same thing as Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are different institutions, different organs. And what is characteristic for these four or five days is that lots of people, some out of fear and some for other reasons, I don't know, it wasn't only those cases. I mean people attached any kind of importance, whatever they felt was best for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that footage from the conference room, the voice that you said was not yours, also mentions the Crisis Staff of SAO Semberija and Majevica. Does that pertain to the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bijeljina? Does that mean that that is the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's predicated upon a -- either a misunderstanding or a misrecollection of the transcript. My specific recollection of the transcript - and I can pull it up now - is that there's a reference to a representative of the Crisis Staff and a representative of the SAO Semberija and Majevica, so two different and distinct references.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, could we please play that part then, P6211 I think is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, if you could identify the time slot and the transcript page number, Mr. Tieger. Why don't we see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure, Mr. President. That's found at about 1.56. -- I would say it starts about 1.56.45 or so, and it's pages 8 and 9 of the -- bottom of page 8 and beginning of page 9 of the transcript. And we -- as indicated, we sent that for review, I don't know if it's been uploaded, but I think some portion is rendered as unintelligible, but in a different version I think we have when it continues the indications I made earlier, that is, the reference to both the representative of our Crisis Staff and the representative of the government SAO Majevica Semberija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we have an updated version of the transcript, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think this is something we need to review after court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Let's play it. I'm not sure -- just a second. I'm not sure if the interpreters have this updated version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Reid thinks so. I was going to suggest -- I just don't know the answer at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's see.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We have to wait for the bishop. "Not necessary. "No, no, I'm not going to explain the situation, the protocol."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This voice that is not yours and Mauzer's probably, is that voice speaking on behalf of the Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina or in some other capacity?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is certainly Mr. Ljubisa Savic's voice and the Prosecution can probably check that. I see that they mention Simic saying something here in this English version. It is certainly Ljubisa Savic's voice and he mentions the Crisis Staff and the president, government of Semberija Majevica - what was that? - and this again has nothing to do with the organs of the municipality of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked on page 34 of today's transcript about the end of June, a new quorum being established of 70 MPs. Can you explain in which situation on the basis of statute how can a new quorum be established, and how did that happen in the first place?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lawyers were preparing this decision probably in accordance with the statute and other documents. Nobody challenged the statutory decision of the municipality of Bijeljina, I presume, and this happened in a situation when some Assemblymen, I assume, either do not want to attend or cannot attend sessions of the Assembly when they're not there. I think that that is the reason why this decision was passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. First of all, that is, again, not an accurate recapping of what the witness was asked about. He wasn't asked about a quorum. He was asked about a document that said what the Assembly shall consist of. Now the accused is attempting to transform it into an entirely different matter and the witness seems to be going along with it. If we want to call up the document to make that clear, that's 1D15015 where it says explicitly the Assembly shall consist of 70 deputies and that's the question I asked, and that's what was confirmed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also take a look? We don't need this footage any longer. Can we have this 1D015 [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, probably we need to switch to e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood correctly, this is already in evidence but that's not the right document, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not it, but is it already an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When Mr. Tieger referred to it, he referred to the 65 ter number of the Defence, so I'm not sure it was -- they were admitted or not. But --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Those exhibits bear Exhibits D1442 and D1445.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, but when Mr. Tieger referred to 1D105 and 1D5011. Correct, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in line 2 it says 1D1505 [as interpreted]. That's what confused me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've been able to call it up as page 4 of 1D15015.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in the decision which says explicitly that the Assembly will be made up of 70 deputies. That's what I'm reading in Mr. Tieger's question, line 3. Which number is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's right. That's page 4 of 1D1515; right? Sorry, 1D15015.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4, please, now, if this is the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what made you prohibit this on the 25th of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute. We are in a mess. I am told that the Registry cannot publish this. We'll put it on the ELMO. I see the last sentence of Article 2, the Assembly shall consist of 70 deputies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can put my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, what changed with this statutory decision?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will read item 2: "The Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina is made up of deputies of Serb ethnicity -- made up of deputies of Serb ethnicity of the hitherto Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina elected at multi-party elections and deputies of the hitherto Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina who chose to work in the Assembly."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is changed then?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the Assembly's made up of 70 deputies. It's important to decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How is it called in our language when you determine the number?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean quorum?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what made you on the 25th of June, 1992, to issue this order? What was the ethnicity of the armed groups to which this applied?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prosecution put this first and I believe I started saying that this order, like another one that existed, applied to armed people in Bijeljina at the time, mainly Serbs were armed, and it could have applied only to those armed formations which were not legal. And it applied according to our interpretation to a paramilitary, or rather, parapolice unit sent by the federal SUP. The Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina prohibited that unit from coming to Bijeljina, although I believe that was not carried out, and this decision was taken on the 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who led that group?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group was led by Davidovic, first name Milorad or Mico.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about him and that group?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing much to say. We had that same situation throughout the period in Bijeljina wherein all sorts of groups came to engage in all sorts of things under I don't know what jurisdiction, but they were not under anybody's command. Command in the army was by the East Bosnia Corps. The rest was in the competence of the Council for National Defence, but throughout the war we tried to treat any other units as paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D15017 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D15017. That cannot be uploaded either, can it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is of the same day. You were rather productive, prolific, on that day. Can you tell us what this conclusion emphasises, what does it establish and why?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose the Ministry of the Interior was sending some unit to Bijeljina, although these two papers from the same session seem a bit contradictory to me. But it confirms what I said. If it's in keeping with the regulations of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in co-operation with the public security station of Bijeljina. That's what I keep saying the whole time. That means units or individuals or groups that were subordinated to the centre of public security of Bijeljina and the military institutions of that organ were considered legal. All the others were illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What made the government and the ministry take this decision to send a special unit of the MUP to Bijeljina? What was supposed to be done there so that they made that decision and you supported it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember specifically anymore what the immediate reason was, but generally speaking if it was in accordance with the hierarchy and the proper jurisdiction, we did not make any problems. I cannot remember the immediate reason. It could be all sorts of things. There were all sorts of incidents throughout the period, although less so in Bijeljina than around the front lines and in neighbouring towns. But most of those paramilitary units liked to come to Bijeljina because they were comfortable there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you name some of those neighbouring towns?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zvornik and Brcko, they were in the zone of war operations and there were direct clashes there. Bijeljina was not directly in that area of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since this was adopted on the same day, were they perhaps concerned to send this special unit in order to enforce the prohibition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Leading. And now we've really moved beyond the scope of the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Leading, absolutely, but well within the scope of the cross which dealt with how they took care of paramilitaries in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it didn't -- dealt with paramilitaries at the beginning of April, in fact, and it didn't -- it didn't go into the events of late June. But in any event, the objection still holds with respect to leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, most problematic is the way the question was put, very much leading and difficult how it arose from the cross because of that matter. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot agree because Mr. Tieger put this document and put questions related to the end of June, and the witness made a distinction saying this has nothing to do with what happened in early April. It's the Prosecution who started on this, but I'm not going to insist anymore. The fact is the witness recognises his own document and I tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have English translation. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, were you familiar with the position of the state authorities and especially my position regarding paramilitary units and irregularities in the operation of state organs?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the position of the leadership and your own position. At that time there were frequent international meetings concerned with establishing peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina and one of the priorities, I believe, both on the ground and in Bijeljina was to prevent the activities of such groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about my own position, did you know it? Did you know what I was demanding and advocating?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know now specifically, but I believe that was also your position but that came a bit later. We had in Bijeljina one problem, namely, that because of these conflicts in Bijeljina and later in the towns around it, that the BH had stopped operating, functioning, in the territory of Bijeljina, not only in our town. The regional centre in Tuzla would cut off our telephones or our electricity. The whole area of Bijeljina did not have telephones working for several months, and in that period we were literally cut off from the outside world. And we had to deal with our problems without the help of the central authorities, we were forced to by the situation in Bijeljina itself. So that the activities of Republika Srpska and Bosnia and Herzegovina started in our area only in May, whereas we had to do certain things already in April in keeping with the guide-lines given by the Serbian republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. On page 3, a video was played showing that man whom you did not recognise; however, he mentioned the Handzar division. Do you know what he meant? Is it something you know?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Handzar division was a fascist unit during the Second World War in our region and there were rumours that these -- this unit -- I don't know whether those are rumours or there's any truth in it, there was some rumours that some similar unit was being or about to be formed again back in our times, but I have no confirmation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic, for coming to testify and for having been such a good leader.

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for this belated praise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to -- we would like to ask two documents to be admitted that were referred to by Mr. Tieger. One of them was referred also by Dr. Karadzic. And those are pages 4 through 7 of document number 1D15015. We can upload it so that those other pages are taken out because they've already been admitted under other numbers. So if it's possible either to admit this as one document or as two, but we would like those pages 4 through 7 to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Probably not, but let me just take a look at what those are. So if -- I mean, if I can take a moment to do that, I don't think that's -- the urgency is really pressing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If necessary, there may be further questions, Mr. Simic. Please bear with us a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll give the Defence number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3136, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Simic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And next witness is Mr. Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mihajlovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello, Mr. Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Hello, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to make pauses between question and answer and to speak slowly. I am one of those who speak very quickly, but here I'm learning for the sake of record to mend my ways so that we wouldn't miss anything.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And also please make pauses between my questions and your answers. Mr. Mihajlovic, have you given a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D7940 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see the statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you also have a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that the Chamber will allow you to use it when you are asked something about specific paragraphs. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the last page so that the witness would identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this statement truthful to what you told the Defence team who conducted an interview with you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is just one typo in paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance. Can we please show paragraph 12. Can you help us by telling us what should be changed there.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: It says here in June 1994 I was appointed chairman of the Executive Committee of the Bijeljina SO and I held this position until late 1994. It should rather say until September 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Up until," and then this should be deleted and it should read "September 1997"; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything else that needs to be corrected?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you the same questions today, would your answers be substantially the same?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this statement, Your Excellencies, in accordance with the Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3137, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read in the English language a short summary of Mr. Svetozar Mihajlovic's statement. [In English] Mr. Svetozar Mihajlovic was the president of the Bijeljina Municipal Executive Committee from June 1994 to September 1997. Before this he was the financial director of the Duvan-Bilje Enterprise in Bijeljina. He lived in the multi-ethnic Bijeljina and was surprised to hear that the trade union protests in the Elvako factory in 1990 and 1991 were organised by the SDA leaders. This he considers that this was done to damage the good relations between the Serbs and the Muslims and to allow the SDA to carry out further separatist activities. Svetozar Mihajlovic learned from two Muslim colleagues on 30th of March, 1992, that a war would start in Bijeljina that night; however, he did not believe them. Later that evening armed clashes occurred in the -- and there was a blockade of some parts of town. I think I made mistake, 31st of March. It was clear that Muslims had been planning this attack and a number of Serb residents did not know what was going on. Svetozar Mihajlovic also learned from his neighbours that the SDA had been handing out weaponry -- weapons from -- to gathered Muslims earlier that day. These thoughts frightened the Serbian residents. Mr. Svetozar Mihajlovic did not think that the army and the police were able to protect them, and so, to save themselves, Serbian residents decided to leave town and to go to the neighbouring villages. They had to leave avoiding the blockades as they were controlled and guarded by well-armed Muslims who illegally checked the IDs of the inhabitants of Bijeljina and would stop them passing the barricades. The SDA leadership had blocked the entire town by setting up numerous barricades and snipers were active all over the town on dominant buildings. Svetozar Mihajlovic was aware of Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, who was a notorious manipulator. On 2nd of April, 1992, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic informed other members of the Presidency that there had been a massacre of Muslims in Bijeljina. A report was ordered and Svetozar Mihajlovic watched Zeljko Raznatovic present this report to President Karadzic even though the stand of the Main Staff of the VRS was very known in relations to units that were not under the control of the VRS. I suppose it's concerning 1995. As the leader of the local commune and a member of the Municipal Board of SDS in Bijeljina, Svetozar Mihajlovic never received any instructions or orders from the republican organs to carry out planned deportation of non-Serbs from Bijeljina, nor did he ever personally issue such an order to his staff. Relations between the civilian authorities and commands of the VRS units in the municipality were correct. The civilian authorities of Bijeljina municipality never interfered in command over VRS corps units. After the fighting of the executive -- after the fighting, the Executive Committee took care and made an effort to create normal living and working conditions for all the citizens of the municipality. They tried to prevent and eliminate any forms of pressure on or crimes against non-Serbs in the municipality, demanding that the local institutions stop and punish any perpetrators of such crimes. In fact -- the fact that the war had led to religious and ethnic polarisation, the extremely poor financial and social situation of the inhabitants of the municipality, the ever-growing number of Serbs displaced from Central Bosnia, and the impossibility to control all the incidents that occurred led an increasing number of Muslims to request to leave municipality -- Bijeljina municipality to go either, temporarily, to an area under the control of BH army or to foreign countries. That is a short summary and at that moment I do not have questions for Mr. Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While your summary does not form part of the evidence at all, page 67, transcript page, from line 4: "A report was ordered and Svetozar Mihajlovic watched Zeljko Raznatovic present this report to President Karadzic even though the stand of the Main Staff of the VRS was very known in relations to units that were not under the control of the VRS." And I read witness's statement paragraph -- statement para 10 and 11. So it was not -- a bit unclear to me. So could you lead live with this witness with respect to this part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihajlovic, you mentioned that you knew that Zeljko Raznatovic was a notorious manipulator and you mention a meeting he had with me in Bijeljina in 1995. If you have your statement with you, please have a look at paragraphs 10 and 11. Would you tell us what you had in mind and describe the event for us.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the fall of 1995 the Serbian Volunteer Guard whose commander was Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, was present in Bijeljina. It was in the morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You do not need to look at the statement of yours. But yes, Ms. Gustafson, was that your point?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That was my point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you tell us from the memory. And if necessary, with notice, you may look at your statement. But I would like you to try to tell us from your memory, as far as you remember. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I found it unusual that Mr. Raznatovic's unit remained in town on that day, especially as it was already several hours since he had arrived in Bijeljina. I could see that he wanted Mr. Karadzic to greet his unit in Bijeljina. Mr. Raznatovic knew, as he was coming to Bijeljina from the front near Sanski Most, that Mr. Karadzic was visiting the bishop of Zvornik and Tuzla in Bijeljina together with the whole leadership. And at any cost, he wanted his presence in Republika Srpska, that is to say at the front near Sanski Most, to be verified in a way by Mr. Karadzic coming out of the building and greeting his unit. I found this strange because I was aware of the position of both the civilian and the military authorities; namely, that units such as the Serbian Volunteer Guard and other paramilitary units which were present in the territories under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska in the beginning would have to decide whether they wanted to be integrated in the Ministry of the Interior or the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is your testimony that the event was not planned at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was certainly not planned in advance, and therefore he as a notorious manipulator - and we know him from earlier, from the first days of the conflicts in Bijeljina - when he did this by skilful manipulation. Therefore, having learned that Mr. Karadzic was present, he went several times, as I learned later on, that he went several times to Vladika's place and asked Deacon Zarko whether the meeting would last long and saying that he needed to see President Karadzic and it was answer to him that the meeting would last long and Mr. Karadzic could not be informed about this. But he in any way took the opportunity at the end of the meeting when Mr. Karadzic went out into the courtyard, he used this opportunity to invite Mr. Karadzic to greet the unit which was lined up at the moment in front of this building of the lower court in Bijeljina. I was watching that from my office which is perhaps a dozen metres away from the street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you by any chance have the opportunity to see the video-clip of this event later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that it, Mr. Karadzic? You concluded your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. I don't think I have any questions at the moment. I could ask him if --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have anything else in mind when you said he was a manipulator?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had in mind the events which occurred in early April when a delegation from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina arrived in Bijeljina led by Mrs. Biljana Plavsic who was a Presidency member. He then also used this opportunity. He lined up his unit in front of the entrance to the Municipal Assembly building. He reported to Mrs. Plavsic, came to her, kissed her, and then together the two of them walked into the Municipal Assembly building. This is also something that's recorded in a video-clip. It was shown around the world and the impression was that Biljana Plavsic and Zeljko Raznatovic were old acquaintances. However, according to the testimony or the book of Biljana Plavsic, and I also directly talked to her on several occasions, saw Arkan for the first time in her life on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. As you have noted, Mr. Mihajlovic, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in most part in writing, i.e., through your statement in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Ms. Gustafson, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to start by -- thank you. I'd just like to start by hopefully clarifying something that Dr. Karadzic mentioned in his summary which was the date when you stated that armed clashes began in Bijeljina. And according to paragraph 3 of your statement you said that armed clashes began on the evening of the 30th of March, 1992. The Chamber's heard evidence that, in fact, those clashes began on the evening of the 31st of March, 1992. I refer to P2629 as an example. So my question for you is: Do you think he may be mistaken and, in fact, the clashes began on the 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the conflicts began on the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Much of your statement is taken up with a discussion of Arkan and your view, as you mentioned again a few moments ago, that he was a notorious manipulator. And you also give a fairly detailed account of events in Bijeljina in early April. But what you don't say anywhere in your statement is that Arkan entered Bijeljina between the 31st of March and the 1st of April with a group of his forces, he took part in the conflict there, and within a few days he had asserted control over the town. Now, that's a pretty important fact about war time events in Bijeljina, a fact that the Trial Chamber should be aware of. You agree?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is no doubted that Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, arrived in Bijeljina on the 1st of April and stayed there for around five days.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you talked about a conversation you had with Biljana Plavsic regarding Arkan's presence in Bijeljina, and the gist of that was that Mrs. Plavsic told you that she had never seen or heard of Arkan until the conflict broke out, and that's at paragraphs 8 and 9 of your statement. When was that conversation you had with Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I had this conversation with her after the events and practically whenever we met, and we met many times. Whenever we would go over these events, Biljana Plavsic would always tell me and always repeat this as an instance of manipulation, this occasion and this image which was represented in such a way that she was really the one who was manipulated. And that Zeljko Raznatovic deliberately, as his positions and actions from the time even before the conflict are well-known, he was very crafty and he wanted, by doing this, to verify himself, to have a justification for himself, so that the impression would be that he had arrived with his unit with the knowledge of the highest government organs even though that was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said that she told you -- Mrs. Plavsic told you that she was the one who was manipulated by Arkan, basically imposing himself on her at this time. But at the time what she did publicly in addition to kiss Arkan, as you have already mentioned, was that she gave an interview on television with Arkan sitting by her side and she stated in that interview that she had decided to leave the rest of the Presidency delegation, visit the Serb Crisis Staff, and meet with Arkan and his associates. And the direct quote is: "It was my choice to first visit the local Serbian people's Crisis Staff and meet here with Mr. Arkan and his associates here." And that's P5587. Were you aware of that public statement by Mrs. Plavsic at the time?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The statement was broadcast in the media. However, one cannot see from the statement that she earlier had any contacts with Mr. Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan. When he came there and met him and realised that he was the man who had arrived in Bijeljina, she wanted to see for herself what the situation was like because she had information that a massacre had been carried out in Bijeljina and that there was a chaotic situation. So she wanted to see for herself together with other members of the Presidency who were members of the -- who were members of the delegation with her and I remember that it was a day of the Muslim holiday Bajram, so that Fikret Abdic, then Mr. Doko, who was in charge of people's defence, and General Prascevic, that is to say a Muslim, were also visiting Bijeljina on that day. So they toured the town and visited some of the Muslim houses for a while. They wanted to see for themselves what the situation in Bijeljina was, whether there were any casualties, how many casualties there were, who the casualties were, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And did Mrs. Plavsic ever tell you that about three weeks after she met with Arkan in Bijeljina she called his headquarters and asked that Arkan come to Sarajevo and "bring the merchandise" and that's P1106. Did she ever tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No, she never told me that, nor have I ever heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. The next thing I'd like to do is actually play the video from 1995 with Arkan but I note the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Because that video-clip was referred to again where Mrs. Plavsic said that she visited the Crisis Staff to meet Mr. Arkan. Could I ask the CLSS to translate that -- officially translate that part of Mrs. Plavsic's word from the video, whether it's 5587 or -- I'm sorry -- or Exhibit P6211.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I note the time. If it is convenient, we shall take a break for 45 minutes, and resume at 1.15. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could just introduce to the Trial Chamber Narges Miraj from Afghanistan who is also one of our legal interns and will be joining us this session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Gustafson, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to play a clip of the event that you described in the autumn of 1995 in Bijeljina with Arkan and President Karadzic. If we could play -- this is P2858 if we could play the first 30 seconds first.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mihajlovic, can you confirm that this is a video of the event that you describe in your statement in the autumn of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could now go to 1 minute and 30 seconds of this exhibit and we'll play until 2 minutes and 7 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "For the guard and for you as the commander of the guard. "Thank you very much, Mr. President. "Gratitude for you being there. This is not ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At page 70 of today's transcript, Mr. Mihajlovic, you testified that this event "was certainly not planned in advance." Now, you said you were a dozen metres away at the time, so I assume you saw President Karadzic hand these two certificates to Arkan, one for Arkan and one for unit. Did it cross your mind at the time that this event would have had to have been planned in advance in order for President Karadzic to have these certificates prepared and ready to hand to Arkan?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I observed this event from my office, which you could see in the footage a moment ago. You could see the municipal building. Perhaps it was about 50 metres away as the crow flies. I heard -- I saw President Karadzic as he was walking from the residence towards this street and I saw Arkan welcome him. I saw when they reviewed the troops and when they kissed the flag, and I heard Mr. Karadzic say "bless you heros" and when they responded. As for this detail, I did not hear this conversation with them. I saw that they stayed there briefly a bit longer, but I did not see the detail of this decoration. It was only later when I saw this footage on television -- actually, it was broadcast that Mr. Karadzic as a token of recognition to Mr. Arkan's unit and to him personally handed this decoration over to him. Actually, I'm not sure whether this had been planned or whether this is something that was prepared by some of the services, the staff, and that Mr. Karadzic just took advantage of this opportunity to hand this over to him. I'm not sure that it had been planned in advance.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you agree that someone in Mr. Karadzic's staff must have planned this in advance in order to prepare these certificates; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this event could not have been planned in terms of happening that very moment because no one could expect Mr. Raznatovic's unit to return precisely on that day to Bijeljina. The return was -- well, it couldn't have been planned in advance - I don't know how many days - it happened on that day. And as for the staff to prepare that, they probably took this opportunity to have this handed over to him, this decoration that had probably been prepared in advance.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your evidence that someone in Mr. Karadzic's staff just walked around with certificates for Arkan in the event that they bumped into him somewhere; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not exactly the way you had put it, but it was just this opportunity that was taken, this decoration was probably in one of the services that was there. And this opportunity was taken when this unit visited, this unit that was returning from the front line. It was a convenient opportunity to have this handed over because the visit of Mr. Raznatovic's unit was not something that often happened. He didn't often visit Republika Srpska. This was the second time that the unit of Mr. Raznatovic came to the area of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's play now from 3 minutes and 7 seconds -- sorry, let's play from here until the end of the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Thank you very much, Mr. President. Would you be so kind as to say a few words to the guard. "Radovan Karadzic: I am deeply thankful and I congratulate you and I hope that we will meet again in peace and you will always have a place in the heart of those who you have defended and we will be their dear guests. Thank you. "Mr. President, in the name of the Serbian Volunteer Guard I wish to say two words to you which is that we are ready and if you call us and that we will be back to defend our ancient homeland, to defend our women and children, to defend the Serbian territory and our Orthodox religion. Thank you, Mr. President. "Good day. Very well, Mr. President. We are going back now. I want to thank you once again. "Radovan Karadzic: Good-bye. "We are here, we will come by and we will be in touch."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, a few moments ago you said you heard what Dr. Karadzic said on this occasion and we heard it again here. He gave multiple thanks to Arkan, he congratulated him and referred to him as a beloved defender of the Serbian territory and the Orthodox religion. Now, your evidence was that Arkan manipulated this situation in order to legitimatise his presence in the RS, but you would agree, would you not, that Dr. Karadzic's choice of words on this occasion, multiple thanks, congratulations in reference to Arkan as a beloved defender, would have added to any impression this event already created about the legitimacy of Arkan's presence in the RS?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask that not to amalgamate what I said and what Arkan said. I did not refer to defence of the faith.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You can answer the question now, sir.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, these are words of courtesy when spoken. I don't see that they carry some big message or anything like that. These are words of courtesy when this unit was returning from the front line. This was a matter of courtesy, a customary thing, to express one's gratitude in that way in that situation, and that's what I have to say. I have to say that the position of the leadership of Republika Srpska and the president on several occasions through his orders, as I've already said, asked for this and cautioned that all units be placed either under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska or the Ministry of the Interior. Since there were conflicts and there was disagreement between Arkan and General Mladic, Arkan's unit did not join the Army of Republika Srpska and was not part of that army. But there was this compromise solution to be within the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, and as such they were considered part of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. A few moments ago you said something long the lines of this was the second time Arkan's unit was present in the RS. Now, are you aware that Arkan was actually in Bijeljina at another meeting around this time, in fact, on the 20th of September, 1995, and in Bijeljina there he met with local Bijeljina officials as well as high-level representatives of the Serbian MUP and the RS government and they were planning an operation to liberate Teocak. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting, but I did hear that Arkan with part of his security detail had been in Bijeljina and not only then. From time to time he would cross over and come to Bijeljina too on his own only with his immediate security escorts to see some friends, et cetera. I heard that some action had been planned vis-a-vis Teocak; however, I think that this action was not fully realised. I think that there were just some attempts, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter 24695, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this is a report from the East Bosnia Corps command security department to the VRS Main Staff and it describes a meeting of the Bijeljina Municipal Assembly attended, among others, by Mr. Frenki and Bozovic from the MUP of Serbia and Arkan on the one side and Mr. Kozic, the RS prime minister, and Minister Boro Bosic and organs of authorities of the Bijeljina region on the other. And at this meeting it was allegedly agreed that Arkan and his unit should take a liberate Teocak. This would be financed and paid for by the republican government and cost 3 million Deutschemarks. Now, I take it from your earlier answer that you are familiar generally with the fact that this meeting took place, although you didn't attend it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Later on I heard that there had been some meeting, but I never heard of this information that I see here now. This is the first time that I see this and this is the first time that I hear of some amount of money being agreed upon, although that is what this document says.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just go to the next page in the English and this is at the bottom of the second-last paragraph in the B/C/S. And here the East Bosnia Corps command states: "Considering the proximity of Teocak to the safe area of Tuzla and the current military and political situation, this operation could also have strategic importance and therefore it deserves an assessment and a decision at the VRS Main Staff level." Now, you gave evidence about your view of the Main Staff's and the VRS's view of Arkan. Were you aware of the fact that the East Bosnia Corps command was recommending to the VRS Main Staff that this operation involving Arkan should be assessed and decided at the Main Staff level?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the question is not fair as it's been interpreted to me and to the witness. That is not what this document means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put your question again just for clarity.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My question was whether Mr. Mihajlovic was aware that the East Bosnia Corps command was recommending to the Main Staff that this operation involving Arkan should be assessed and decided at the Main Staff level. And I think that's a completely fair question based on this document.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand in this document at least that this had to do with the Serb Volunteer Guard, that is one thing, at least on this page I do not see that. And Teocak was a strategic location throughout and several times during the conflict attempts were made to resolve the issue of Teocak; however, this never succeeded and the Army of Republika Srpska never took Teocak. Although certain problems came from there, certain attacks and so on. Maybe General Simic here asked for consent from his superiors, but I know that permanently there was this conflict between Arkan and General Mladic. He did not recognise him and he didn't want his presence in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I don't think the witness has been able to confirm anything about the document and it's also not inconsistent with his testimony because it's -- he said he didn't know and it isn't something he would have been expected to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, two responses to that. First, I think the witness did generally confirm that he was aware of such a meeting taking place; and secondly, it does have impeachment value. I note that in relation to my last question this witness had said given his views on the VRS Main Staff view of Arkan and this document states clearly that the East Bosnia Corps command is recommending to the Main Staff that they consider and assess and make a decision on this operation that the document states will involve Arkan and his unit taking and liberating Teocak. So I think it does have impeachment value as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Ms. Gustafson. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6210, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Mihajlovic, I'd like to move on to another topic. At paragraph 21 of your statement you commented on an adjudicated fact about a plan implemented in September 1992 to rid Bijeljina of its remaining Muslims, a plan that involved killing remaining Muslim families, and your comment about this fact was that it was completely false. But you don't deny, do you, that Muslim families were killed in September 1992? For example, the murder of the members of the Sarajlic and Sejmenovic families by Dusko Malovic's special police unit was common knowledge in Bijeljina at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Something did happen when paramilitary units committed a crime in a neighbourhood in Bijeljina called Bukres. Two families were taken and two other families I think, so there were about 20 persons there. This was an abominable thing that happened, and all of Bijeljina and Semberija had condemned that as unacceptable. However, no one can say that this as a planned crime and no one can say that it happened in several places in town. This was just in one place in one part of town where this thing that happened was truly terrible. But one cannot say that it was planned, that it was organised, that it was planned in advance and this kind of thing happened in several parts of town in order to exert pressure against the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said that paramilitary units committed this crime. This crime was widely attributed to Dusko Malovic's special police unit, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Dusko Malovic was represented as some kind of regular unit that had come. We in Semberija and Bijeljina, we the official leadership, considered it to be a paramilitary unit and we never accepted it was a regular unit because it did not have any credibility with us. And we did not accept that unit. On the contrary, we reacted on the basis of all of that that happened with a view to having this unit removed from Bijeljina as soon as possible, and that was done, indeed. This crime that they committed was later dealt with by the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina and still is before that court.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it was dealt with much, much later, right, many years after this event?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that's right. Units, or rather, officials of the MUP carried out an on-site investigation and saw what the situation was, and other organs that were supposed to deal with this straight away, they probably did not act. I was not in government at the time, in Bijeljina, but later on an investigation was started with regard to all of that and I believe that this process -- I hope that this process is being brought to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to have D1429 on the screen, please. And the document you're about to see is the document you discuss at paragraph 14 of your statement. This is the document where you request -- you and others request that criminal proceedings be initiated against Vojislav Djurkovic also known as Vojkan. First I'd like to ask you about your statement because the first statement we received of yours, the one that you gave to Defence investigators before you arrived in The Hague referred to this document and in that statement you said that this document was an example of how the Executive Committee demanded that local institutions stop and punish the perpetrators of crimes. Then after you came to The Hague you added three lengthy passages to this paragraph and you -- in those passages you explained that, in fact, this document doesn't reflect any underlying criminality at all and you gave an elaborate story about how this was all a big misunderstanding, that the Pale authorities were informed, General Subotic came to Bijeljina to investigate. Mr. Djurkovic was arrested and said that he was assisting Muslims over Mount Majevica and that the Muslims in Bijeljina organised some kind of protest to complain about Djurkovic's arrest. I'd like to ask you because I would think that if what you told to the Defence after you came to The Hague about this document is, in fact, true, I would think that when you were first shown this document by the Defence, the first thing you would have said was: This is all a big mistake. We thought Vojkan was expelling Muslims but we conducted an immediate inquiry and we found out that, in fact, he was assisting Muslims over Mount Majevica at their own request. Can you explain why you failed to say any of this when you were first shown this document by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: There's something in your question that I did not say, actually, nor is it in my statement. These are different incidents. Vojkan Djurkovic was a person on that committee that was conducting exchanges, in fact, perpetrating abuses and moving Muslims out of Bijeljina. That's an action that we in the government condemned and we were all opposed to what he was doing. And that is why when one in a series of these incidents happened we who are signed here below demanded that Mr. Djurkovic be brought in before us to explain on whose behalf he was doing it. As you can see from the document, that was right after the day when this group of Muslims were driven out. And in that group there was some people who wanted to go but there were also people who did not want to leave their homes, and that was precisely the problem. He very often abused his position and rounded up even those people who had no intention of leaving. That's why we did what we did. Those who wanted to leave were offended because this action we had organised was terminated. He told them: If you want, you can go and protest it. And some of them really came to protest when we said that he should stop doing this and that otherwise we would arrest him. After that, a group came to protest before the Municipal Assembly. Certainly they did not speak for everyone. But there were Muslims who wanted to leave to reunite with their families or leave for third countries or simply wanted to leave out of fear because at that time there was a great crisis in Bijeljina, there were many refugees, so many that the population was doubled. The pressure was enormous. People were looking for accommodation. And in this search for residential space incidents and even crimes happened. And we were trying to prevent this, that's why we said that we would arrest him if he goes on. There are other decisions by the War Presidency that I signed calling for precisely such measures that we took against Vojkan and against other groups that were trying to disturb our interrelations in this way and were putting pressure on Muslims to leave Bijeljina or expel them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to make sure I have this clear. It's your evidence that Vojkan did, as you said, often abuse his position and round up even those people who had no intention of leaving. So it's your evidence that Vojkan was expelling Muslims from Bijeljina, although not every Muslim who left Bijeljina with Vojkan was expelled. Is that a correct understanding of your position?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. However, among those who left Bijeljina in the organisation of Djurkovic there were certainly some people who did not want to leave. But none of the reports from those Muslims who were leaving Bijeljina ever came to the official authorities against Djurkovic. He is still free. He was under investigation for a while, but he was released because nobody officially reported him, although -- although we had indications that he was, indeed, involved in wrong-doing and that some of the people whom he made leave did not want to go. He was acting outside the party, contrary to the policy of the party and in co-operation with Mr. Arkan. He was, in fact, under Arkan's control. He was a member of Arkan's unit who remained in Bijeljina. I heard later that there were some verbal duels between them in Bijeljina. Arkan wanted him to make a financial contribution for the upkeep of his unit in Erdut. Vojkan gave him some money, but Arkan thought it was not enough. And that's where they had a verbal clash. All that was done was done bypassing the authorities and the ruling party in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Do you have re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions. Could we look at P6210 that was admitted a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until it appears, can you tell me, Mr. Mihajlovic, do you know who Boro Bosic was?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Boro Bosic was the manager of the Ugljevik mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could we zoom in on the Serbian version, the last paragraph, zoom inasmuch as we can to see the nature of this document. Can we collapse the English. The parties can still see it. I will read this. It says: "I notified the commander of IBK General Simic, Eastern Bosnian Corps. The information was received from a reliable source and it was not verified. I will try to verify it in future and keep you informed of anything I find out." Can you tell me, what kind of information is it and what does it mean, "obtained from the source"?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously this is information that is not even remotely direct knowledge, and based on that information, based on that report, the author says that he will try to get some more information or to verify it and report later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say Mr. Bosic was the director of this hydro power-plant, did you know this even without him? What would be his interest in releasing the water reservoir?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because it is an integral part of the hydro power-plant for the hydro power-plant to operate normally, in view of the threats that the reservoir would be emptied, disabling the hydro power-plant, it's certain that Mr. Bosic would have found it in his interest to remove that danger and to secure the reservoir so that the hydro power-plant could operate continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The minister of energy, Prime Minister Kozic, and Mr. Bosic, were they able to issue orders to carry out this strategic operation? Could they make the decision?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. That would have been in the jurisdiction of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago when you were asked about dealing with these crimes in Bijeljina much later, you answered that the MUP made an on-site investigation and documented the crime. Did the MUP do it immediately?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: MUP officers started working on the case immediately, determined the number of victims, put on record all the facts, and reported to their superiors. I have no details. I know only that this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that Arkan's unit perpetrated any crimes in Krajina in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not. And I believe no information was available about that. Arkan was involved in an operation around Sanski Most, and that, to the best of my knowledge, is connected with his involvement in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you remember and can you tell the Chamber all the forces that attacked Republika Srpska in the autumn of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1995 Republika Srpska was attacked in addition to the BH army by the regular army of Croatia with its paramilitary units that participated in these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was -- were they assisted by an international military organisation with air-strikes and logistics?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Certain strategic targets in Republika Srpska were bombed at the time and that was the harbinger of further action to facilitate the passage of the BH army and the regular army of Republika Srpska. They were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I fail to see how this arises from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it explains one of the reasons why Arkan may have been present in Bijeljina in 1995, which was a subject covered by the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. During the cross-examination there were questions about Arkan's involvement in other areas of Bosnia and that he was coming back or was present in Bijeljina after having participated in the war in 1995 and other areas of Bosnia. So the reasons for that participation -- and I think the witness has testified that he was under the MUP as opposed to the VRS during that period. So I think that the reasons for his presence in 1995 in Bosnia was something that was -- came out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how is an international military organisation related to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, because in September 1995 when Arkan was in Bosnia, Bosnia was under attack by NATO, by Croatia, and the Krajina was falling during that period. So I think that's the relevance of it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have anything to add, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. Just that -- well, I mean -- I guess -- it was the -- the evidence about Arkan's presence in Bijeljina was raised in direct, it was in the witness's statement, and then I questioned about that presence in Bijeljina and nothing about any wider context. So I don't think this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber's fine with dealing with Arkan's participation, but the question was formulated to the effect whether there's any international organisation with air-strikes and logistics. What does it have anything to do with Arkan's participation? So could you put your question more directly in a not-leading way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mihajlovic, you said that Arkan's unit, not he and his entourage, was in Republika Srpska only twice. What exactly did you mean? What was the first time and what was the second time?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The first time was on the 1st and the 2nd of April and he stayed until the 5th, I believe, in Bijeljina. That's the first time, as far as I know. And the second time was in September 1995 in Krajina in the environs of Sanski Most and that area. I don't know exactly how many days he stayed there. Anyway, at that time, in that area, there was an aggression going on, an attack on Krajina by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by the regular army and paramilitary units of Croatia, and the advance operation to that, the Operation Storm, was the bombing of Serb positions and towns by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During her [as interpreted] first stay, is it the case that Bosnia and Herzegovina of which we were all part was still in existence? Do you remember when it was internationally recognised?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: At that time it was still the state of Yugoslavia, and Bosnia was recognised by the United Nations later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So could we say that September 1995 was his first visit to Republika Srpska. Before that his first visit to -- was to the Republic of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice my presence in Bijeljina or any telephone communications from me during the April events?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No. At that time you never appeared nor did you make any comments. At that time at the insistence of the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, a delegation was set up. And during those days two different delegations from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us one last thing. What kind of information did the Presidency and the foreign minister Salajdzic and the official Muslim representatives present about the number of victims in the April events? You spoke about that on page 74 today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, I don't think -- it has nothing to do with any of the questions that I asked. The only thing I asked about April were the -- first, clarifying the date that the conflict started and the questions about Mrs. Plavsic's contacts with Arkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, can you answer how this arose from the lines of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it arises because the witness was not allowed to finish his answer. On page 74 he tried to say that Biljana Plavsic and Abdic came to ascertain whether a massacre had really happened because there was talk about a large number of victims, but he was interrupted. I'm now giving him a chance to answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- what kind of massacre it was, what kind of number are we talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let me check the transcript. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: First of all, there's no indication that the witness was cut off in his answer or failed to complete his answer. And secondly, I would note that at paragraph 9 of his statement he already said that Mr. Izetbegovic informed other members of the Presidency that there had been a real massacre of Muslims in Bijeljina. That's why the delegation went to Bijeljina. So if Dr. Karadzic had wanted to ask more -- find out more about this report, he could have asked it in his direct or clarified it in the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But these lacunas in the transcript clearly show that the witness did not express himself exactly as he wished. However, I have no further questions and I thank you very much, Mr. Mihajlovic, also for your work while you were part of the authorities in Bijeljina, and for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Mihajlovic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next witness that we have scheduled is not here and I released him for the day because of my expectation as to the time as well as his age, and I didn't want to have him waiting around. Yesterday we had a witness who waited for four hours and VWS asked me to be more considerate of the witnesses. So I apologise for having to rise early, but I assure you it won't affect our ability to complete the witnesses within the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. Yes. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 21st day of March, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.09 p.m.,
